sources.headline: Coalition’s migration plan risks breaching India free trade agreement and damaging economy, advocates warn
sources.text: The Coalition’s migration plan risks breaching Australia’s free trade agreement with India, signed by the former Morrison government, allowing Indian students to stay and work for up to four years after completing their studies.Angus Taylor on Tuesday announced plans to cut net overseas migration to 100,000 for the first two years of a Coalition government and up to 160,000 in year four, in a plan which would abolish temporary graduate visas, make major cuts to international student, bridging and temporary protection visas, and halve humanitarian places.Under the plan, temporary graduate visas would be slashed from 271,200 to just 10,000 by 2031-32.The shadow home affairs minister, Jonno Duniam, said any graduate wanting to remain in Australia would have to return home and apply for a separate temporary visa.“Universities and other educational institutions have reverted to, sadly, selling a pathway to some form of permanency or perhaps even citizenship rather than education; that’s not what this scheme was set up for,” Duniam said.“Abolishing the temporary graduate visa … means we can focus on skills we need in this country, not just whatever is churned out of our universities.”Duniam said there would be a four-year transitional phase before the abolition of the temporary graduate visa. Some workers in priority areas such as health, education and in some regional areas would be allowed to remain.Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter herePhil Honeywood, the chief executive of the International Education Association of Australia (IEAA), said this could breach the India free trade agreement.A letter on the agreement, from the then Liberal trade minister Dan Tehan, in April 2022, states: “Australia agrees to maintain the following opportunities for former students to live, study and work in Australia temporarily after finishing their studies.” This includes allowing trade or diploma graduates to stay up to 18 months, bachelor graduates up to two years, bachelor graduates in Stem courses and master’s graduates up to three years, and doctoral degree graduates up to four years.Honeywood said it was “ironic” the Coalition was targeting the visa when it had negotiated special conditions with India, the second largest cohort of international students in Australia, behind China.He warned Australia would lose skilled workers in critical areas under the Coalition’s changes.He said Australia would take “money off bright young people for their qualifications” before sending them home without having the chance to benefit from their high-demand health, IT and engineering skills.Honeywood said the explosion in non-genuine international students coming to Australia was in part due to a post-Covid directive by the then Liberal prime minister Scott Morrison, who increased the number of hours international students could work in key industries.“[Morrison] opened the floodgates to non-genuine students coming out of Covid without consulting the sector, promising more work rights for international students while they were meant to study full-time,” Honeywood said.A Coalition spokesperson told Guardian Australia there would be no treaty breach, and the party would look at establishing different visa pathways for some of those graduates.skip past newsletter promotionafter newsletter promotion“Our treaty commitments are to provide temporary visa pathways for some students to stay post their study for short periods. Which visas are provided is up to Australia,” the spokesperson said.“When we implement this policy in government we will work through with affected international partners which new visa pathways, including skilled visa pathways, their citizens can access.”Australia announces immigration changes, including new visa policy for foreign students – videoThe Coalition’s plan would cut international student commencements to 240,000, below the current planning level of 295,000. But a spokesperson for the assistant minister for international education, Julian Hill, said the sector was now tracking towards 250,000 commencements for this calendar year.Universities Australia said the changes risked doing “lasting damage” to Australia’s higher education sector and the economy. In a statement, its chief executive, Luke Sheehy, said removing the temporary graduate program could make Australia less attractive for students.“Restricting post-study work rights also risks making Australia less competitive for talented students and graduates at precisely the time we need more skilled people contributing to our economy.”Hill said removing the temporary graduate visa would make Australia a less attractive option and deny the country the ability to “select the brightest skilled graduates and would hurt Australian employers and industry”.He said all comparable nations had competitive postgraduate work opportunities.“Wiping out temporary graduate visas would mean many of the brightest students will simply never choose Australia, further trashing our fourth biggest export.”

sources.headline: Australia's migrant policy offers lessons for EU and US
sources.text:
Nations that send asylum seekers to third countries for offshore processing and holding could spend billions, only to face accusations of human rights abuses and financial mismanagement, as in Australia.
The European Union has nevertheless been considering the idea, and the United States has already made similar third-country deals, but Australia has been processing or relocating people outside the country where they seek protection for more than two decades.
Former Australian Prime Minister John Howard introduced the so-called Pacific Solution in 2001, targeting immigrants who arrived by boat, and establishing Australian migration processing centers with the help from governments in Papua New Guinea (PNG) and the tiny island nation of Nauru .
Thousands sent to islands under Australia's 'Pacific Solution'
Center-left and center-right governments described the policy as a deterrent, saying people were less likely to attempt dangerous ocean crossings or pay smugglers if arriving by boat did not provide a route to Australia. In his 2001 election policy speech, Howard said the famous line, frequently quoted since: "We will decide who comes to this country and the circumstances in which they come."
In 2008, a newly elected Labor Party government phased out the practice, saying it was a cynical, costly, and ultimately unsuccessful exercise.
But faced with more deaths at sea, a Labor government under Prime Minister Julia Gillard started sending maritime arrivals to Nauru and Manus again in 2012, after an expert panel recommended reopening the centers.
"I'm not going to play politics or look at political scoreboards when too many lives have been lost," Gillard said at the time.
Between 2013 and 2014, the number of people transferred offshore peaked to more than 3,000.
Journalists have been mostly barred from the centers on Nauru and Manus Island. Graham Thom, Advocacy Coordinator for the Refugee Council of Australia (RCOA), told DW that this lack of access and independent oversight meant many Australians accepted the narrative that the policy was working. Australia has been sending aslyum seekers who arrive by boat to Nauru for more than 20 yearsImage: Medecins Sans Frontieres/AP Photo/picture alliance
EU considers offshore arrangements
People without a legal right to remain in the EU could face deportation to third countries as soon as 2027, with Rwanda and Uzbekistan reportedly under consideration as third-party countries, as well as Uganda.
The European Parliament in June approved new rules that would pave the way for so-called "return hubs" outside the EU's borders.
Denmark's Minister for Immigration and Integration, Morten Bodskov, told reporters last month the hubs would not be detention and deportation centers.
"We are not talking about camps," Bodskov said, describing the scheme instead as "a new chance to have a life in a partner country."
Denmark, alongside Germany, Austria, Greece, and the Netherlands, known collectively as the Group of Five, said in September they had agreed on steps towards a deal with a non-EU country, without naming it.
The group was to speak with the United Nations , the International Organization for Migration and the UN Refugee Agency about their next steps.
The proposal allows for harsh penalties for those who refuse to be removed to the hubs, including detention for up to 30 months pending deportation from the EU and entry bans.US already has a third-country migration scheme
The US government has already made deals with at least 30 third countries in Africa and Latin America. In June, Amnesty International said some agreements had been revealed through the US Freedom of Information Act, while others "remain secret."
The US Supreme Court ruled late last month that the second Trump administration could resume deportations under the third-country scheme, after a US appeals court ruled that immigrants must receive effective notice of their intended destination and an opportunity to challenge removal if they fear persecution or torture.
The first deportations from the US under the third-country removal scheme were of immigrants convicted of crimes, but more recently, foreign nationals not accused of any crime have also been deported.
Trump deportees to Cameroon face life of uncertaintyTo view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Accusations of human rights abuse
Asylum seekers and human rights advocates have repeatedly alleged human rights abuses in Australia's offshore migration processing program, with Thom describing the policy as a "medieval idea."
A group of asylum seekers formerly detained on Manus Island reached a AU$70 million (€43.47 million/$48.47 million) settlement in 2017 after filing charges for abuse and unlawful detention.
In February, an Australian Senate inquiry heard first-hand witness accounts of neglect, untreated health conditions, and serious concerns for the safety and dignity of camp inhabitants — especially of women being kept on Nauru. Prior to the hearing, 73 UN member states had publicly raised concerns about Australia's migration policies.Australia and Nauru have agreed on a billion-dollar deal for certain convicted foreign nationals to be deported to the Pacific Island nationImage: Dominic Giannini/AAP Image via AP/picture alliance
Brazil, China, Finland, Germany, Serbia, Switzerland and Turkey called for an end to offshore processing of asylum claims.
Australia has yet to officially comment on the recommendations, but successive governments have said offshore processing helps deter dangerous boat journeys, with former Prime Minister Tony Abbott describing the policy during his term as "decent, humane and compassionate."
The effect of offshore processing is difficult to isolate from other policy measures, especially the practice of turning back asylum boats. This "turnback" policy was introduced and reintroduced under conservative governments in 2001 and 2013 respectiv
